summary.text: The biggest risk is that the contract bans patient health data from leaving the US, yet AtliQ's Pune team handles it, which could lead to termination, breach notification and credit monitoring costs, and HIPAA fines that no contract cap limits.

findings.title: PHI banned outside the US, but the Pune team handles the data
findings.quote: No PHI shall be accessed, stored or processed outside the United States.
findings.whatItMeans: Only US-based AtliQ staff, named in writing to the client, may touch patient data (see also [3.1]). Staff outside the US may see de-identified data only, inside the client's US systems. The deal says the AtliQ Pune team touches the data. If Pune staff see PHI, AtliQ breaches this BAA from day one. As a Business Associate, AtliQ would also be directly exposed under HIPAA. There is no transfer route to India because the contract forbids it. This BAA is already signed.
findings.whatItCouldCost: A cure notice and possible termination of the MSA under [10.2]. Breach notification and credit monitoring costs under [5.4]. Contract claims up to the [9.1] cap. HIPAA regulators can fine AtliQ directly, and those fines are not limited by any contract cap.
findings.howToSoften: Act now, before any Pune access. Option 1: staff PHI work with named US personnel and give Pune only de-identified data inside the client environment. Option 2: ask the client for a written amendment under [11.1] allowing named offshore staff to access PHI only inside the US-hosted Covered Entity Environment (virtual desktops, MFA, no download). Get legal advice before relying on either option.

summary.text: The biggest risk is a one-way, uncapped indemnity to the whole client group, made worse because the contract requires data to stay in the US while AtliQ's Pune team will work on it, which could mean unlimited costs far beyond the USD 92,000 fee and the USD 1M cyber policy.
Second, the delay penalty of 1% a day ($920) has no cap, applies even when the client causes the delay, and comes on top of any other damages the client can prove.

Do not sign until the indemnity is capped and mutual, the data location issue is fixed, the delay penalty is capped and excused for client-caused delays, and IP passes only after payment; also ask for copies of the missing client policies.

findings.title: Uncapped delay penalty: 1% of the Contract Value per day
findings.quote: the Supplier shall pay to the Customer liquidated damages in the amount of one per cent (1%) of the Contract Value for each day or part day
findings.whatItMeans: There is no ceiling on what AtliQ pays for being late. AtliQ's usual is 0.5% of the milestone fee per week, capped at 5%.
findings.whatItCouldCost: $920 a day; reaches the full $92,000 fee in 100 days.
findings.howToSoften: Cap the total at 5% of the affected milestone fee, charge per week not per day, and make it the client's sole remedy for delay.

findings.title: Penalty applies even when the client causes the delay
findings.quote: the Supplier shall pay to the Customer liquidated damages in the amount of one per cent (1%) of the Contract Value for each day or part day
findings.whatItMeans: Nothing excuses AtliQ when the client is late with access, data or approvals — AtliQ still pays the penalty.
findings.whatItCouldCost: At Brightwater the client gave access 19 days late and AtliQ still paid the penalty.
findings.howToSoften: Add: "No liquidated damages are payable for any delay caused by the Client, its personnel or its other vendors."

findings.title: Penalty is not the client's only remedy for delay
findings.quote: in addition to any other right
findings.whatItMeans: The client can take the penalty and also sue for its actual losses. AtliQ's usual makes the penalty the sole remedy for delay.
findings.whatItCouldCost: Open-ended: the penalty plus any damages the client can prove.
findings.howToSoften: Add: "Liquidated damages are the Client's sole and exclusive remedy for delay."

findings.title: IP passes to the client on creation, before payment, and covers all outputs
findings.quote: All intellectual property rights in the Deliverables shall vest in the Customer on creation.
findings.whatItMeans: The client owns everything AtliQ produces as soon as it is made, even if unpaid. 'Deliverables' means all outputs of the Services, not only items made specifically for this client. Generic components, data models or code AtliQ builds during the project could pass to the client. AtliQ's usual term is ownership on payment, for client-specific work only.
findings.whatItCouldCost: AtliQ could lose reusable work for good. It would have no IP leverage if the client terminates (clause 16.3 requires handover of work in progress) or does not pay.
findings.howToSoften: Change it so ownership passes on full payment. Limit it to deliverables created specifically for the Customer. Make clear that generic know-how, tools and components stay with AtliQ under a licence.

findings.title: Data must stay in the US, but AtliQ's Pune team will work on it
findings.quote: The Supplier shall not process Customer Data outside the United States without the Customer's prior written consent.
findings.whatItMeans: The work is delivered by AtliQ's team in Pune, India, and they will touch the client's claims, policy and payments data. Without the client's prior written consent, AtliQ breaches this clause as soon as the Pune team accesses the data. A breach of clause 13 triggers the uncapped indemnity in clause 15.1.
findings.whatItCouldCost: Unlimited indemnity exposure. The client could also terminate for breach.
findings.howToSoften: Get the client's written consent to processing from India before any data access. Put the consent in a signed variation (clause 19.3). Name the Pune team and the security controls.

findings.title: One-way, uncapped indemnity to the whole client group
findings.quote: The Supplier shall indemnify the Customer and each member of the Brightwater Group against all losses
findings.whatItMeans: AtliQ must cover 'all losses' of the client and every company in its group. This covers data or confidentiality breaches, IP claims and AtliQ's negligence. The client gives AtliQ no indemnity in return. Nothing reduces AtliQ's share where the client's own fault contributed. Clause 15.3 leaves this outside the cap.
findings.whatItCouldCost: Unlimited. A data incident involving insurance claims and policyholder data could cost far more than the USD 92,000 contract value and the USD 1M cyber policy.
findings.howToSoften: Make the indemnity mutual. Limit it to third-party claims. Reduce it to the extent the client or its group caused the loss. Put it under the liability cap, or a fixed cap matched to insurance.

findings.title: Brightwater Group policies notified to the Supplier is referred to but missing

findings.whatItMeans: The contract incorporates Brightwater Group policies notified to the Supplier, but it was not provided. AtliQ would be agreeing to terms it has not seen.

findings.howToSoften: Ask for Brightwater Group policies notified to the Supplier and review it before signing.

findings.title: Time is of the essence for every Key Date
findings.quote: Time shall be of the essence in respect of the Key Dates.
findings.whatItMeans: Missing any Key Date, even by one day, can be treated as a serious breach. This could let the client terminate and claim damages, on top of the daily penalty.
findings.whatItCouldCost: Loss of the contract and the remaining milestone fees after a minor slip.
findings.howToSoften: Delete 'time shall be of the essence'. Or limit it so that only a long delay caused by AtliQ, for example after a cure period, counts as material.

findings.title: Client sets the acceptance tests and there is no deemed acceptance
findings.quote: subject to acceptance tests determined by the Customer
findings.whatItMeans: The client alone decides the tests. There are no agreed criteria. Nothing says a deliverable counts as accepted if the client stays silent after 15 Working Days. Because payment depends on acceptance (clause 7.2), the client controls when AtliQ is paid. Clause 8.2 requires fixes within 10 Working Days at no charge.
findings.whatItCouldCost: Delayed or withheld milestone payments. Repeated free rework.
findings.howToSoften: Agree the acceptance criteria in Schedule 1 in advance. Add deemed acceptance if no written rejection with reasons arrives within 15 Working Days. Allow rejection only for material failure against the agreed criteria.

findings.title: 24-hour security incident notice
findings.quote: within twenty-four (24) hours of becoming aware of it
findings.whatItMeans: AtliQ must report any security incident affecting client data within 24 hours. The time difference with Pune makes this tight.
findings.whatItCouldCost: An easy breach of clause 13, which triggers the uncapped indemnity.
findings.howToSoften: Ask for 48 to 72 hours. Or require an initial notice within 24 hours with details to follow, limited to confirmed incidents.

findings.quote: free from material defects for a period of twelve (12) months after acceptance
findings.whatItMeans: AtliQ must fix defects for 12 months after acceptance. Work is judged against 'Good Industry Practice', which clause 3.1 defines as the standard of a 'leading supplier'. That is a high bar.
findings.whatItCouldCost: A long period of free fix work after the project ends. Higher risk of claims about quality.
findings.howToSoften: Cut the warranty to 90 days. Make fixing the defect the only remedy. Define the standard as a reasonably skilled supplier.

findings.quote: Subject to clauses 9, 15.1 and 15.4, the Supplier's total liability under this Agreement shall not exceed one hundred and fifty per cent (150%) of the Contract Value.
findings.whatItMeans: Bounded, but above AtliQ's usual cap of 1× the fees (9 of 12 contracts).
findings.whatItCouldCost: Up to $138,000 instead of $92,000.
findings.howToSoften: Ask for 1× the fees; accept up to 1.5× only if the deal justifies it.

findings.title: work in progress unpaid
findings.quote: On termination, the Supplier shall deliver all work in progress and Customer Data to the Customer.
findings.whatItMeans: AtliQ can be dropped and is paid only for accepted deliverables, not work in progress. AtliQ's usual is 30 days with work done and in progress paid.
findings.whatItCouldCost: Unbilled work in progress at the time of exit is lost.
findings.howToSoften: 30 days' notice; pay for all work done and work in progress up to the termination date.

findings.title: Insurance demanded: $2,000,000 (21.7× the deal)
findings.quote: professional indemnity insurance of not less than USD 2,000,000
findings.whatItMeans: AtliQ's cyber and professional-indemnity cover is about $1M. This asks for $2,000,000.
findings.whatItCouldCost: Buying extra cover could cost more than the margin on the deal, or AtliQ is in breach from day one.
findings.howToSoften: Offer AtliQ's existing $1M cover, or cap the requirement in proportion to the deal value.

findings.title: Every client group company can enforce the indemnity and data terms
findings.quote: each member of the Brightwater Group may enforce clauses 12, 13 and 15
findings.whatItMeans: Any company in the client's group, not just the contracting company, can sue AtliQ directly under the confidentiality, data and indemnity clauses.
findings.whatItCouldCost: More possible claimants for the uncapped indemnity. AtliQ may face claims from companies it has never dealt with.
findings.howToSoften: Remove third-party rights. Or require any group claims to be brought only through the Customer and counted under one shared cap.

findings.title: Foreign governing law: England and Wales (Courts of London, England (exclusive))
findings.quote: governed by and construed in accordance with the law of England and Wales.
findings.whatItMeans: Disputes would be decided under England and Wales in Courts of London, England (exclusive), where AtliQ has no presence. AtliQ's usual is a US state's law.
findings.whatItCouldCost: Defending or enforcing a claim abroad means foreign lawyers and travel — often more than a small claim is worth (the Brightwater lesson).
findings.howToSoften: Ask for a US state's law, or neutral arbitration (e.g. SIAC) as a fallback.

summary.text: The biggest risk is that AtliQ would have unlimited liability for any NDA breach, with no cap anywhere in the contract (clause 6.2), and because patient and hospital data is in scope, a single leak could pass regulator penalties under the DPDP Act, patient claims and Meridian's own costs to AtliQ with no upper limit.

Second, although it is called "mutual," the NDA only binds AtliQ (clauses 2.1, 3.1 and 5.1), so Meridian could freely use or pass on AtliQ's know-how, proposal ideas or pricing, including to competing vendors, and once that information is out it cannot be taken back.
Do not sign until the indemnity is capped, since AtliQ's hard line is never unlimited liability, and the confidentiality obligations are made to bind both sides.

findings.whatItMeans: Only the other side's information is protected. Anything AtliQ shares — architecture, pricing, methods — is not.
findings.whatItCouldCost: AtliQ's know-how disclosed in discussions can be used or passed on freely; once out, it cannot be taken back.

findings.howToSoften: Make every obligation mutual: "each Party" as both discloser and recipient. AtliQ only signs mutual NDAs.

findings.title: Uncapped indemnity for any NDA breach, with no liability cap anywhere
findings.quote: The Recipient shall indemnify Meridian against losses arising from any breach of this Agreement by the Recipient or its personnel.
findings.whatItMeans: AtliQ must cover all of Meridian's losses from any breach by AtliQ or its staff. Nothing in the NDA limits the amount. Clause 6.1 also keeps Meridian's right to damages on top. Only AtliQ gives this promise.

Limit the indemnity to direct losses caused by AtliQ's proven breach. The PDF is marked as executed, so any change will need a signed amendment.

summary.text: The biggest risk is that the contract relies on a Business Associate Agreement that is missing (clause 2.3), so AtliQ cannot check its data-protection obligations or fines, and no data should move until that agreement is settled.

Second, AtliQ's responsibility for leaks by anyone it shared information with has no money cap (clause 3.2), so damages could in theory be unlimited, and the client may also seek a court order without posting bond (clause 7.1).
Do not sign or share any data until the Business Associate Agreement is provided and agreed, and negotiate a money cap on liability for breaches by recipients.

findings.title: Business Associate Agreement is referred to but missing
findings.quote: shall be disclosed only after execution of a Business Associate Agreement between the Parties
findings.whatItMeans: The contract incorporates Business Associate Agreement, but it was not provided. AtliQ would be agreeing to terms it has not seen — and these govern how personal data is handled.
findings.whatItCouldCost: Data-protection obligations (and fines) AtliQ cannot check; data must not move until it is agreed.
findings.howToSoften: Ask for Business Associate Agreement and review it before signing.

findings.title: Responsibility for breaches by recipients has no money cap
findings.quote: Each Party is responsible for any breach of this Agreement by persons to whom it discloses Confidential Information.
findings.whatItMeans: AtliQ is answerable for any leak by its staff, Pune affiliate, contractors or advisers. The NDA sets no limit on damages for that. The clause is mutual, and uncapped NDAs are common in the market. Still, it departs from AtliQ's rule that liability is never unlimited. The client's security documentation (named in [2.1]) is the kind of material that could lead to large claims if leaked.
findings.whatItCouldCost: In theory, damages for a leak by anyone AtliQ shared information with are unlimited. The client may also seek a court order without posting bond under [7.1].
findings.howToSoften: Many clients will not accept a cap in an NDA. Practical steps instead: share the client's materials only with a small named team, keep the [3.1] written confidentiality agreements on file, and ask for a mutual exclusion of indirect or consequential damages if the client is open to it.
